fields.title: A person doesn't read everything all at once
fields.keyTakeaway: At each step of attention, a person has a specific question, and you must answer the current one. A message that answers everything at once answers nothing.
fields.checkQuestion: Why shouldn't you write the same thing on a banner as on a pricing page?
fields.blocks/0/text: The same question about value, but adjusted for **how much attention a person has right now**.
fields.blocks/1/items/0: **Attention** — noticed. Task: match the reader's situation in a single phrase.
fields.blocks/1/items/1: **Interest** — interested. Task: show that the task can be solved at all.
fields.blocks/1/items/2: **Desire** — wanted. Task: prove that it works specifically for them.
fields.blocks/1/items/3: **Action** — took a step. Task: remove everything preventing them from clicking.
fields.blocks/1/items/4: **Satisfaction** — got what was promised. Without it, the previous four turn into churn.
fields.blocks/2/text:
A banner in a Telegram channel for accountants: "Does an acceptance certificate take a week by mail?" — that's attention, a question about the situation, nothing about the product.

Landing page: "In-browser signing, without EDI operator or trips" — interest.

Pricing page: case study of a 12-person company, 6-hour signing time, price — desire.

Button: "Try 14 days, no card needed" — action, removing friction.

If you put pricing page copy on the banner, it won't work: the person hasn't asked "how much does it cost" yet.
fields.blocks/2/title: Reestr, one message across four steps
fields.blocks/3/text: AIDA describes a linear path that most people don't take: they arrive on recommendation directly at pricing or return a month later. The fifth step — Satisfaction — is more important than the other four, and it lies outside marketing: it's the product itself.
